delta_name: Wire delay and wire variation dominate setup closure
at_28nm: Timing closure often behaved as if cell sizing and logic restructuring could absorb interconnect effects; pre-route and global-route timing correlated reasonably well with post-route results.
at_7nm_5nm: Post-route timing is dominated by net topology, placement proximity, layer choice, via stacks, and local RC variation. Small placement moves can change critical path slack by order tens of picoseconds.
why_it_changed: Metal pitch scaled faster than interconnect resistance and via/contact resistance improved. Narrower wires, dense vias, and tighter spacing increase wire RC and make wire delay more variable.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer tries to fix post-route setup violations by upsizing cells and sees little improvement or worse TNS. Long critical nets stay negative until placement, layer assignment, or useful skew is changed.
workflow_impact: More timing-driven placement, net-length budgets, useful-skew planning, and post-route ECOs. Extracted-parasitic timing must be consulted earlier and more often.

delta_name: Congestion shifts from channel capacity to pin and via access
at_28nm: Congestion often looked like macro-channel or global routing capacity. Widening channels, moving macros, or adding tracks could recover much of the problem.
at_7nm_5nm: Hotspots often arise at cell pins, macro pins, and via stacks. Detailed-route DRCs can be severe even when global-route overflow looks modest.
why_it_changed: Smaller metal pitch, stricter via rules, limited pin shapes, and end-of-line or coloring rules reduce effective access to pins and lower layers.
what_breaks: The engineer trusts low global-route overflow, then detailed route fails with many pin-access and via violations. Widening channels does not fix the problem because the bottleneck is access, not gross track count.
workflow_impact: Pin-access-aware placement, detailed-route feasibility checks earlier, macro pin planning, and via-driven DRC analysis become part of placement signoff rather than post-route debug.

delta_name: Lithography rules and coloring make routing less free
at_28nm: Routing could treat metal layers as relatively regular resources. DRC was mostly spacing, width, area, and simple antenna rules.
at_7nm_5nm: Multi-patterning or EUV-driven constraints add coloring, same-color spacing, end-of-line, pattern density, and wire-spreading requirements. A legal route depends on interactions among nearby nets, not just local clearance.
why_it_changed: Lithography limits require pattern decomposition or complex pitch rules. Minimum spacing and pattern density constraints couple adjacent wires, so routing resources are not interchangeable.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer packs wires tightly to relieve congestion, then sees coloring conflicts, end-of-line failures, or pattern-density violations. Ripup and reroute oscillates because the obvious alternative tracks are not legally usable.
workflow_impact: Pattern-aware or color-aware rule decks, early DRC-driven routing, and more conservative track usage. Congestion metrics must include legal-route capacity, not just nominal track count.

delta_name: Hold closure becomes harder and more coupled to clock planning
at_28nm: Hold often closed with buffer insertion and simple min-delay fixes after setup closure.
at_7nm_5nm: Hold is sensitive to clock skew, statistical variation, low voltage, cell transitions, and useful skew. Hold fixes can create congestion, setup loss, or new violations elsewhere.
why_it_changed: Statistical local variation, asymmetric rise/fall behavior, tighter clock uncertainty, and dense routing make min-delay paths less predictable and more coupled to clock tree shape.
what_breaks: The engineer inserts hold buffers late in the flow. Detailed route becomes more congested, setup timing degrades, and hold violations reappear after incremental routing or clock changes.
workflow_impact: Hold analysis must occur during CTS and placement, not only after route. Skew tuning, min-corner validation, and post-route hold ECOs become planned steps.

delta_name: Clock distribution shifts from simple trees to meshes and local skew control
at_28nm: Balanced clock trees with global skew targets were common. Large clock buffers could often be placed relatively freely, and clock DRCs were manageable with standard tree structures.
at_7nm_5nm: Clock planning uses meshes, fishbone structures, clustered sinks, multibit clock gating, and controlled useful skew. Clock power, DRC, and hold sensitivity dominate the clock plan.
why_it_changed: Higher clock power, dense standard cells, worse wire RC, and hold sensitivity make naive trees inefficient and risky. Local skew becomes a resource and a liability.
what_breaks: A 28nm-style tree with aggressive global skew causes clock DRCs, hold failures, or excessive clock power at 7nm/5nm. The clock tree may meet skew on paper but fail min timing or routing.
workflow_impact: Clock architecture is defined before placement, placement is clock-aware, and post-CTS signoff includes skew, hold, clock DRC, and power. Incremental clock ECOs are expected.

delta_name: IR, EM, and dynamic power integrity become first-class constraints
at_28nm: Power grids were often sized statically and checked late. Local IR fixes or extra straps could sometimes be added after routing without destroying the design.
at_7nm_5nm: Dynamic IR drop, electromigration, and low-voltage noise are planned with the floorplan. Late power-grid changes are expensive because they disturb routing, timing, and DRC.
why_it_changed: Higher current density, thinner wires, lower supply margins, and many power states increase resistive drop and reliability risk. Timing margin is too small to absorb large dynamic voltage droop.
what_breaks: The engineer delays power-grid reinforcement and sees timing collapse under dynamic IR, EM failures, or late strap insertion destroying routing resources.
workflow_impact: Early power-grid planning, dynamic IR analysis with representative vectors, EM signoff, and decap/strap co-optimization become recurring implementation steps.

at_28nm: A manageable set of PVT corners with OCV or AOCV derates often sufficed for setup and hold signoff.
at_7nm_5nm: Signoff includes many PVT/RC corners, statistical variation models, aging effects, and sometimes combined voltage-temperature-aging scenarios. Corner selection itself is a project risk.
why_it_changed: FinFET and interconnect variation, local mismatch, reliability requirements, and reduced timing margins increase uncertainty and the number of conditions that can be worst-case.
what_breaks: The engineer signs off only historically familiar corners. Silicon misses frequency, leakage, or reliability targets, or the team later discovers that a omitted corner dominates setup or hold.
workflow_impact: Corner matrix planning, statistical variation analysis, corner pruning with justification, and much more STA compute management become explicit signoff tasks.

delta_name: Utilization targets moved down because routability no longer scales with cell density
at_28nm: Higher standard-cell utilization was often achievable if global-route overflow was controlled and macro channels were sized reasonably.
at_7nm_5nm: Effective utilization targets are lower or more uneven. Dense regions require extra margins for pin access, clock buffers, power, and DRC legal spacing.
why_it_changed: Standard-cell density scaled, but routing tracks, vias, and legal DRC space did not scale proportionally. Congestion becomes access-limited rather than purely track-count-limited.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer pushes high utilization to save area. Detailed route fails with pin/via DRCs and timing cliffs even though global overflow and average utilization looked acceptable.
workflow_impact: Early density feasibility studies, local density screens, macro channel planning, and route-capacity-based placement goals become more important than simple utilization targets.

delta_name: Vt mix and cell selection become multidimensional optimization
at_28nm: Vt assignment was often a coarse leakage-versus-speed tradeoff with a few cell classes, applied in relatively large regions or after synthesis.
at_7nm_5nm: Multiple Vt options, threshold flavors, and cell height choices interact with leakage, timing, area, DRC, and electromigration. Vt swapping is used continuously through closure.
why_it_changed: Leakage and power density targets require granular threshold options, while performance targets require selective use of faster cells. Process and library support more variants than in older nodes.
what_breaks: Blanket LVT use fixes setup but fails leakage or power targets; blanket HVT use fixes power but creates setup failure. Late Vt swaps can cause timing regressions or DRC issues if cell geometry or pin access changes.
workflow_impact: Iterative Vt optimization across synthesis, placement, CTS, routing, and signoff. Power-aware timing and leakage constraints become first-class closure targets.
